title: Chromatic Number for Infinite Graphs
content: The chromatic number $\chi(G)$ is defined as the infimum of cardinals $\kappa$ for which $G$ admits a proper $\kappa$-coloring. For finite graphs this recovers the familiar minimum color count. For infinite graphs it becomes a cardinal: $\chi(G) = \aleph_1$ means $G$ cannot be properly colored with countably many ($\aleph_0$) colors but can be colored with $\aleph_1$ colors. The predicate `hasAleph1ChromaticNumber` captures graphs at this specific level of uncountable chromatic complexity, which is the minimum possible uncountable chromatic number under the axiom of choice.

title: Infinite Connectivity via Disjoint Paths
content: A graph is infinitely connected if any two distinct vertices are joined by infinitely many pairwise internally-disjoint paths. This is formalized through a layered definition: `PathInGraph` (a list of vertices with consecutive adjacency), `DisjointPaths` (no shared internal vertices between two paths), `PairwiseDisjoint` (all pairs in a set are disjoint), `InfinitelyManyDisjointPaths` (an infinite such set exists between given endpoints), and `InfinitelyConnected` (this holds for all vertex pairs). By Menger's theorem (infinite version), infinite connectivity is equivalent to having infinite vertex connectivity — no finite vertex cut separates any two vertices.
mathContext: $G \text{ is infinitely connected} \iff \forall u \neq v,\, \exists \{P_i\}_{i \in I} \text{ with } |I| = \aleph_0,\, P_i \text{ pairwise internally disjoint } u\text{-}v \text{ paths}$

title: The Erdős-Hajnal Question (1966)
content: `ErdosHajnalQuestion` formalizes the original 1966 conjecture by Paul Erdős and András Hajnal: if $\chi(G) = \aleph_1$, must $G$ contain an infinitely connected subgraph $H$ with $\chi(H) = \aleph_1$? The intuition was that high chromatic number should force rich connectivity structure — a graph needing uncountably many colors should contain a highly connected 'core' also needing uncountably many colors. The answer turned out to be NO: one can build graphs where the chromatic bottleneck lives in thin, poorly connected regions.

title: Three Counterexamples and an Edge Variant
content: Four axioms record the disproof timeline: (1) Komjáth (2013) showed consistency of a counterexample — in some models of ZFC, such graphs exist. (2) Soukup (2015) constructed an explicit counterexample provable in ZFC alone, using ladder-like structures built from trees. (3) Bowler-Pitz (2024) gave a simpler, more elementary construction. (4) Thomassen (2017) extended the negative answer to edge-connectivity: even requiring infinitely many edge-disjoint paths doesn't force $\chi = \aleph_1$ in subgraphs. Each axiom asserts $\exists G$ with $\chi(G) = \aleph_1$ where every infinitely connected subgraph $H$ satisfies $\chi(H) < \aleph_1$.
mathContext: $\exists G : \chi(G) = \aleph_1 \land \forall H \subseteq G,\, H \text{ inf. conn.} \implies \chi(H) < \aleph_1$

title: ZFC Independence for $\aleph_1$-Vertex Graphs
content: When restricted to graphs with exactly $\aleph_1$ vertices (not just $\chi = \aleph_1$), Komjáth proved the answer is independent of ZFC: in some models there exist counterexamples, in others every $\aleph_1$-vertex graph with $\chi = \aleph_1$ contains the desired subgraph. This is a striking example of set-theoretic independence in combinatorics — a purely graph-theoretic statement whose truth depends on which axioms of set theory one adopts. The independence result uses models with different cardinal characteristics.
mathContext: $|V(G)| = \aleph_1 \land \chi(G) = \aleph_1 \implies \exists H \subseteq G \text{ inf. conn. with } \chi = \aleph_1$ is independent of ZFC
